activities.anchor: Size matters, but so does what covers the ground
activities.caption: call the magnitude — the giant's catchment
activities.name: rivAmazonEstimate

config.prompt: The Amazon's drainage basin is the largest on Earth. Roughly how many million km² does it cover?
config.why: About 7 million km² — the Thames' is 13,000 km² — delivering roughly a fifth of all river water entering the ocean.
config.context: Every drop of rain lands in exactly one catchment; the basin is bounded by a watershed ridge you cannot see on the ground.

activities.caption: file each change: floods sooner and higher, or later and lower
activities.name: rivLagBuckets

config.prompt: Each of these changes a basin's storm hydrograph. File them:
buckets: shortens the lag, raises the peak
lengthens the lag, lowers the peak

items.label: roofs, tarmac and storm drains going in
floodplain restoration that slows the basin's response
a dam regulating the flow downstream

config.why: A forested, permeable basin intercepts rain and releases it slowly; an urbanised basin sheds it almost instantly — and the city retimes and amplifies everyone else's flood downstream, not just its own.

activities.anchor: the numbers follow the Bradshaw model
activities.caption: run the gauging station — discharge in cumecs
activities.name: rivDischargeEstimate

config.prompt: A gauging station measures a channel 12 m wide and 1.5 m deep, flowing at 0.8 m/s. What is the discharge?
config.why: Q = cross-sectional area × velocity: 18 m² × 0.8 m/s = 14.4 cubic metres per second — the arithmetic every river gauging station runs.
config.context: Downstream, width and depth grow and roughness falls, so velocity and discharge rise — the Bradshaw model's surprise.

activities.anchor: The measured picture is close to the reverse
activities.caption: find the faulty line — the course-notes
activities.name: rivBradshawSpot

config.prompt: One line of these course-notes is wrong — click it:
lines: Downstream, gradient falls while channel width and depth grow.
Velocity and discharge tend to rise downstream.
Roughness falls, so less energy is wasted on friction with bed and banks.
The mountain torrent is therefore the fastest water on the course.
The long profile is a graded curve that always aims at base level — sea level.
config.correction: A broad, smooth lowland river moves faster than a boulder-chocked steep one — the mountain torrent wastes its energy on friction.
config.why: Which is exactly why the larger, faster lowland flow can carry sediment all the way to the delta — and why raising base level with a weir or reservoir makes a river dump its load upstream.

activities.caption: pair each process with what it looks like
activities.name: rivTransportMatch

config.prompt: Erosion and transport in a working river — pair each process with its signature:

pairs.right: water and air pockets rammed into cracks
fine silt held in the water — why big rivers run brown
sand-sized grains hopping along the bed

config.why: It takes more energy to pick up a large particle than to carry it, and still more to pick up sticky clay than clean sand — the Hjulström curve's key insight.

activities.anchor: adjacent loops pinch through in flood
activities.caption: rebuild the sequence — meander to oxbow
activities.name: rivOxbowOrder

config.prompt: How a meander becomes an oxbow lake — in order from first to last:
items: The river erodes the outer bend and deposits on the inner slip-off slope
Meanders migrate downstream and sideways over time
Adjacent loops pinch through during a flood
The abandoned loop becomes an oxbow lake
config.why: Erosion where velocity and turbulence are highest, deposition where they fall — energy arithmetic, not scenery, which is why the same sequence plays out on every continent.

activities.caption: the river desk — fight the water, or work with it
activities.name: rivHardSoftBranch

config.root: You manage a reach of a large river that has just flooded. The budget covers one direction of travel this decade.

choices.label: Fight the water — build harder
choices.feedback: Concrete has a résumé — and a bill that arrives elsewhere.

choices.label: Work with the system — build softer
choices.feedback: Slower, greener, and it hands some land back to the river.

hard.text: Dams give flood control and power — but trap the sediment that builds deltas downstream. Embankments and levees protect one bank but constrict the channel, raising flood levels next door and downstream: the Mississippi's levees made its floods higher. Channel straightening moves water faster — to someone else's reach.

choices.label: Add a downstream reach to the scheme
choices.feedback: The residual risk has to live somewhere.

soft.text: Afforestation and floodplain restoration slow the basin's response; 'room for the river' schemes — the Netherlands now deliberately lowers embankments and relocates dykes — give floods somewhere to go; warning systems and floodplain zoning refuse to put hospitals on land rivers own. But zoning is political: who is allowed, or forced, to live on the floodplain?

config.why: Rivers cannot be beaten into submission; they can only be bargained with — hard engineering moves risk, soft engineering works with the system, and the best answers weigh them together.

activities.caption: drag the divider — one coastline, fifty years apart
activities.name: rivBanglaCompare

config.prompt: Bangladesh's storm deaths, before and after community-based adaptation — drag the divider:

before.text: About 138,000 dead in a comparable cyclone — deltaic, low-lying, monsoon-fed, one of the densest countries on Earth, with shelters and warnings still to come.

after.label: the 2010s
after.text: Comparable storms now kill hundreds to a few thousand: cyclone shelters and early-warning systems, floating farms and raised homesteads, and a national strategy that treats seasonal floods as an asset — the silt that renews the land.

config.why: Storm deaths cut more than tenfold — the worked case study of a negotiation with the conveyor belt rather than a victory over it.
